newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico analysts watching guerrilla actions closely.
newsitem.headline: Mexico analysts watching guerrilla actions closely.

text.p: Financial analysts in Mexico are watching closely to see if recent guerrilla fighting in the southwestern state of Guerrero spreads to other states or urban areas.
The analysts said the clashes would not make a great impact on Mexico's financial markets as long as they were confined to isolated rural areas.
"It depends on how the situation develops. As long as it is limited to the Guerrero hills, it will not provide any major upsets," leading Mexican economic commentator Enrique Quintana told Reuters.
"If there were urban activity, then that could generate fear among investors and hit sensitive markets, leading to a fall in the IPC stock index and a weaker peso," he added.
Mexican authorities said five people were killed in clashes between the army and rebels from the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) on May 24 and 27.
Gray Newman, an economist with HSBC James Capel, said earlier spates of EPR attacks were more widespread and hit the Pacific Coast state of Oaxaca and the state of Mexico, which borders Mexico City.
"To the extent (the recent fighting) is limited, I don't see it as a reason for investor concern," he said.

Several analysts said there were no apparent links between the guerrilla clashes and mid-term elections due July 7. Nonetheless, ongoing rebel campaigns would make market watchers attach greater importance to political events in general, they said.
"We are in the run-up to elections, so investors will be watching broad political developments," Newman added.
Lars Shonander, head of research at Santander Investment, said, "It makes little sense to link guerrilla activity to the electoral process."

One analyst, who asked not to be named, said the main electoral impact could come from what he said was a tendency by the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) to discredit the center-left Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) over its alleged backing of the EPR.
Many recent opinion polls show PRD candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas as the frontrunner in the first-ever election for mayor of Mexico City.

Shonander said EPR attacks have thus far had little market impact. "I can't imagine it helps, but quite honestly I don't think a lot of market attention is being focused on the matter right now," he said.

Gerardo Copca, an analyst with the Finamex brokerage, said Mexican markets had grown accustomed to guerrilla outbreaks, at least since January 1994, when the Zapatista National Liberation Army fought the Mexican army for 10 days in the southern state of Chiapas before reaching an uneasy truce
"Up to a point, it is not having influence on the market," said Copca. "Guerrilla activity has been present since 1994 and no longer triggers volatility."
He added, "It does cause concern but is not the downfall of the country. We may always have unrest, but that hardly means we will see a turnaround in economic policy."
